data.title: How to specify a digital twin that earns its keep
data.excerpt: Most twins are models looking for a question. A useful one is bounded, maintained, and tied to a decision someone actually makes.
data.body:
A digital twin can mean a CAD assembly, a simulation model, a live asset register, or a statistical forecast. The word is broad enough to hide an unbounded project.

The specification should start with the decision: commissioning a line, planning maintenance, testing a control change, or training an operator. Each requires a different fidelity, update cadence, and owner.

Four questions that bound the scope

  • Which decision changes because the twin exists?

  • What is the minimum fidelity that makes that decision reliable?

  • Who updates the model when the plant changes?

  • How will we know the model has drifted from reality?

Treat the model as an asset

A twin without an owner and a maintenance routine becomes a museum. Define the update trigger — a change request, a shutdown, a sensor recalibration — and test the model against measured behaviour at the same cadence.

The result is less impressive in a demo and far more useful on a Tuesday morning.
